This is a special broadcast this week.
In fact, we have a special guest, Todd Stark, who is director of programs and exhibits for the Discovery Center of Science and Technology in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.
And as you may recall, if you've listened to our shows in the past, you know for probably six or eight weeks now we've been talking about a traveling exhibit of lasers and holograms.
It's coming to the Lehigh Valley area that's been put together by Pacific Science Center.
And we're going to host it at the Discovery Center of Science and Technology.
Well, Todd took some time to come into the studio this week and sit down so that HoloTalk listeners can get firsthand information and some detailed information on what this exhibit is all about.
One of the things that we did not touch on, and I promised Todd I would mention, is there's going to be a smaller exhibit that goes along with this.

And I just want to let you know that that's going to be included also in the exhibit when you would come out to see the main exhibit.
And I had a chance to see the model this week from one of the students.
They put a model together when they applied for the grant.
And it's very nice.
It's a very nice little exhibit that you're going to put together.
So don't forget to check out the Star Trek laser and hologram exhibit that runs along with this if you come out to the Discovery Center.
Excuse me.
So as far as details, Todd's going to fill us in on that.
And there's also a link on the HoloTalk page where you can click on that link.
And there's a page at the Web ZM that I put up today to show you a few pictures that uh were sent out in the press kit and also give you some more information.
And you can get on a mailing list uh for email list.
Every so often we'll send out some information.

So if you want to have all the latest information, just click on the link on the laser and hologram page, and every so often you'll receive an email which will give you updated information on what's happening.
So let's move on to the interview with Todd Stark.
I'm not going to come back on uh at the end, so let me at this time say thank you for tuning in, and here's the interview with Todd Stark.
Okay, we're in the studio uh with Todd Stark, who is the uh director of programs and exhibits at the Discovery Center of Science and Technology, which is in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.
Todd, I want to welcome the whole talk.
Well, welcome.
Thank you, uh Frank.
Thanks for having me.
Um we're going to be talking about the new exhibit that's coming into the area, and it's very exciting.

If you may remember we had an exhibit that traveled through this uh what we call the Northeast Carter um probably a few years ago at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia, which was Lasers, holograms and virtual reality.
And since then we've been in a uh quite a bit of a dry spell.
And it's a wonderful opportunity for everyone in this area to come out and finally have another major exhibit of lasers and holograms in this area.
Now, I know you were involved uh with Kosai, which was the uh touring company behind what the uh exhibit was in f in Philadelphia.
Is there some comparisons, uh things that are the same, things that are different that you could maybe uh let some of the listeners know about?
Sure.
Um well Liquid Vision, which was the uh the official name of that exhibit that was traveled in in Franklin was there uh about three and a half years ago on its opening tour.
And um it was it's very so much centered around the high tech industry and oh by the way had holograms that it showed.

It had a really nice collection of holograms and that this exhibit here, lasers and holograms uh traveled by the Pacific Science Center out of Seattle, Washington, uh focuses more on getting to understand how holograms are created, what you can do with holograms, um, what their interactions are with lasers, the importance of lasers in our lives, um, how they work, how to do laser shows and that.

So in the area of lasers and holograms, this exhibit here is much more interactive than the Liquid Vision exhibition, which tended to stray more toward the the three-dimensional computer graphics and um high tech glitz and and that but dealt very little with the actual holograms themselves.
From what I've been able to see with the the promotional materials that I've had it seems to me that this is happening at just the right time.

Uh some of the past hologram exhibits that had traveled around such as the one in Philadelphia and also images in time and space which did its uh round in Canada and out on the West Coast was more of a wow look at this type of an exhibit.
Now I think we're moving beyond that and we're saying okay we've been wild.
Tell us how is this going to affect our lives?
How is this going to affect our children's decision as far as career someday?
Can my child go out and actually support a family or whatever it is that they want to do in these fields?
And I think that's where we're moving at, and and this is definitely one of the focal points of this exhibit, which is called, by the way, Lasers and Holograms Exploring the Splendid Light.
And it's a touring exhibit by Pacific Science Center.

And uh do you want to take a few moments and do you do you have an idea of what some of these little interactive exhibits are that the people tell us a little bit if someone were to come out and uh I guess they could spend quite a bit of time going around each and every little station, but what are some of the highlights that they can expect to see if they come out to the Discovery Center?
Right.
Well, you know, I happen to agree with you, uh Frank on on the wow factor for holograms, I think is passed.
Uh you know, since we're finding holograms on our driver's licenses and uh credit cards and that, um, there are more and more applications for lasers and holograms.

Um, you know, we we there's going to be, I think there's over 18 large-scale holograms, very impressive um pictures, um, some from holographics north to um private producers and that uh in there, but that's not the focus, that's not the feature of it.
It's it's sort of complementary to the exhibits and hands-on activities that we've got going on there.
Um with this exhibit, uh we look into the world of fiber optics.
You know, lasers and holograms are are linked, of course, really closely, and um fiber optics is the next step in in telecommunications.
Um it's it's most of what's carrying the net as it is now, but very few people have a true understanding of what fiber optics is and that.

So the kids are really going to get in and interact with several different smaller scale components dealing with different facets of of lasers and uh applications of lasers in their everyday lives and the creation of holograms.

I see in the making of the hologram.
In the making of a hologram.
You can look through it and see the hologram image being made on the plate.

Oh that's the interferometer.
Interferometry, yeah, thank you.
That's yes.
And uh that's covered as well.
So there's a lot of great little application.
It's going to be a really fun glitzy ex uh exhibit and we hope to complement it with some some wonderful program programmatic aspects that we'll be developing over the next couple months.
Well maybe maybe we should touch a little bit on what information you have now about some of the in uh educational programs that will be available.

The Discovery Center of Science and Technology is is very dedicated in not just having students come in and see science but experience it and show them how they can move on later in their life as far as career decisions.

Could you tell us a little about that?
That is correct.
We're running of course our week long summer camp as many uh institutions like ourselves do throughout the country.

Um what kind of things, how can they make money, you know, using lasers and and stuff that they think that's really cool.
Uh so exploring those avenues um with our uh six to twelve year olds is is where we're headed with that.
Okay.

Um I'd also like to point out to people that some of the holograms that are going to be on exhibit, believe it or not, didn't start out as just holograms, but began during the photographic process with traditional photography, which are called s uh holographic stereograms.

So if you're a photographer or part of a 3D stereo group which seemed to be cropping up and becoming uh very uh popular lately, uh you definitely want to stop over to the uh Discovery Center and see some of these because some of these holograms originally started with a photographic process, not just holographic.

Um a series of photographs are taken from different perspectives, and then those photographs are processed in the traditional manner, uh, some actually are used uh with digital technology, but they're then brought into the laboratory, and all those different perspectives are actually digitized and brought into the holographic process where you have a uh three-dimensional hologram as the final product.

So uh this is not that far away from photography, and I know we have a lot of uh photography uh clubs and amateur and hobbyist photographers out there, and I I'm sure that you would be absolutely thrilled to see uh what's possible to do with your own camera and then have those pictures made into a three-dimensional hologram.
Um the dates, would you like to tell us about dates and times, uh, hours of operation and how we can uh get in touch with you if you want some more information?
I I know we're gonna put some information on the web.
There's gonna be some information right at the uh webzium for everybody coming through, and the Discovery Center also has uh its own site.
So Todd, why don't you fill us in on how we can get more information on this?
Sure.
Um the Lasers and Holograms uh exhibition will be running this summer.

So be here all summer.
Your chance to check it out.
Um you'll be you can catch us at the Discovery Center uh Tuesdays through Saturdays, uh 9 30 to 4 30 and Sundays 1230 to um 430.

This is uh becoming quite a learning experience.

Yeah, it is pretty cool and it is amazing what they're able to do now uh nowadays.
Um we'll be telling the story of how uh laser shows are are made through the actual laser show itself.
There you go.
There's a unique use.
Uh educational.
We're not just doing it's rock music.
We're not going to be able to do that.

Okay.
